electrolysis-faraday-s1.title: Copper plating a key
electrolysis-faraday-s1.text: A student plates copper onto a brass key. The key and a copper strip dip into 1.0 M CuSO₄(aq) and are connected to a power supply. A steady current of 2.50 A runs for 30.0 minutes. Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). Molar mass of Cu = 63.55 g/mol; F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.

electrolysis-faraday-s2.title: Three cells in series
electrolysis-faraday-s2.text: Three electrolytic cells are connected one after another (in series), so the same charge, 1.93 × 10⁴ C, passes through each. F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.

items.q: How much charge, in coulombs, passes through the circuit?

mistakes.why: Value: you used 30.0 minutes as if it were seconds. Convert to 1800 s first: q = It needs t in seconds.

items.q: Calculate the mass of copper plated onto the key.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cu. Each Cu²⁺ needs two electrons, so divide moles of electrons by 2.
Value: time must be in seconds (1800 s), not minutes.
Value: you multiplied by 2. There are 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cu, so divide moles of electrons by 2.

items.q: Which electrode is the key, and what happens there?
options: The anode, where Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons and copper plates on
The cathode, where Cu²⁺ gains electrons and copper plates on
The cathode, where copper atoms lose electrons and dissolve
The anode, where copper atoms lose electrons and dissolve

why.correct: The key gains copper, so Cu²⁺ is reduced on it: the key is the cathode.
options: Gaining electrons is reduction, which happens at the cathode, not the anode.
Right: plating is reduction, which happens at the cathode.
Losing electrons is oxidation, which happens at the anode.
That is what happens at the copper strip, not at the key.

items.q: How many minutes would it take to plate 2.00 g of copper at the same current?

mistakes.why: Units: that is the time in seconds. Divide by 60 to report minutes.
Value: you used 1 mol e⁻ per mol Cu. Copper(II) needs 2.

items.q: How many moles of electrons pass through each cell?

mistakes.why: Value: divide the charge by F (coulombs per mole of electrons); do not multiply.

items.q: What mass of aluminum is produced in Cell 3?

mistakes.why: Value: Al³⁺ needs 3 mol e⁻ per mol Al. Divide the moles of electrons by 3.
Value: you multiplied by 3. Three electrons are needed for each Al, so divide.

why.correct: 0.2000 mol e⁻ × (1 mol Al / 3 mol e⁻) × 26.98 g/mol = 1.8 g Al.

items.q: Which cell produces the greatest mass of metal, and why?
options: Cell 3: aluminum ions carry the largest charge, so they attract the most electrons.
The three masses are equal, because the same charge passes through each cell.
Cell 2: copper is between silver and aluminum, so it balances charge and mass best.
Cell 1: Ag⁺ needs one electron, giving the most moles, and Ag is heaviest.

why.correct: Same mol e⁻ in each cell; mol metal = mol e⁻ ÷ (electrons per ion), then × molar mass. Silver wins on both counts.
options: A larger charge means more electrons per atom, so fewer atoms form from the same charge.
Equal charge gives equal moles of electrons, but different moles and masses of metal.
There is no balancing; work out each cell: Ag is largest in both moles and mass.
Right: 0.200 mol Ag (21.6 g) versus 0.100 mol Cu (6.36 g) and 0.0667 mol Al (1.80 g).

items.q: What is the ratio of moles of Ag : Cu : Al produced?

why.correct: mol metal = mol e⁻ ÷ charge on the ion: 0.200/1 : 0.200/2 : 0.200/3 = 6 : 3 : 2.
options: Right: 0.200 : 0.100 : 0.0667 mol, the ratio 1 : ½ : ⅓, or 6 : 3 : 2.
This follows the charges, but more electrons per ion means fewer moles of metal, not more.
The moles of electrons are equal, not the moles of metal.
Those are the molar masses; the mole ratio depends on electrons per ion.

items.q: What does the Faraday constant, F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻, represent?
options: The charge carried by one electron
The current that plates one mole of metal per second
The charge carried by one mole of electrons
The voltage needed to plate one mole of metal

why.correct: F is the charge of one mole of electrons: 96,485 C/mol e⁻.
options: One electron carries 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; F is that times Avogadro’s number.
F is a charge per mole, not a current, and the metal plated depends on its ion’s charge.
Right: it converts between coulombs and moles of electrons.
F is in coulombs per mole, not volts.

items.q: A car part is chrome-plated from a Cr³⁺ solution (Cr³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Cr). If 1.80 × 10⁴ C pass through the cell, what mass of chromium (52.00 g/mol) is deposited? (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻)

mistakes.why: Value: each Cr³⁺ needs 3 electrons. Divide mol e⁻ by 3 before converting to grams.

items.q: What constant current deposits 0.500 g of silver (107.87 g/mol) from Ag⁺(aq) in 600. s? (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻)

mistakes.why: Value: that is the charge. Divide by the time, 600. s, to get the current.

items.q: An aluminum smelting cell runs at 1.00 × 10⁵ A for 1.00 hour. Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (26.98 g/mol). What mass of aluminum, in kilograms, does it produce? (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻)

mistakes.why: Units: that is grams. Divide by 1000 for kilograms.
Value: each Al³⁺ needs three electrons. Divide moles of electrons by 3.
Value: 1.00 hour is 3600 s, not 60 s.

items.q: Two students electrolyze molten NaCl (2 Na⁺ + 2 Cl⁻ → 2 Na + Cl₂) with the same current for the same time. Which statement about the products is correct?
options: Equal moles of Na and Cl₂ form, because the same current passes both electrodes.
Twice as many moles of Cl₂ as of Na form, because chlorine is a diatomic gas.
Twice as many moles of Na as Cl₂: 1 e⁻ per Na, but 2 e⁻ per Cl₂.
No sodium forms, because the reaction is not thermodynamically favored.

why.correct: The same electrons pass both electrodes. 1 mol e⁻ makes 1 mol Na but only ½ mol Cl₂.
options: Equal electrons, but 1 e⁻ per Na and 2 e⁻ per Cl₂.
Being diatomic means each Cl₂ takes two electrons, so fewer Cl₂ form.
Right: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na, and 2 Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
An electrolytic cell drives an unfavored reaction; that is its purpose.

items.q: A student plates copper and finds the key gained less mass than calculated from the current and time. Which is a plausible cause?
options: Some current went into another reduction at the cathode, such as making H₂.
The student used a larger key, which needs more copper.
The copper anode lost mass during the run.
The CuSO₄ solution was more concentrated than 1.0 M.

why.correct: Faraday’s law assumes every electron reduces Cu²⁺. Side reactions use some electrons, so less copper forms.
options: Right: if not every electron reduces Cu²⁺, less copper plates than Faraday’s law predicts.
The mass plated depends on the charge, not on the size of the key.
The anode is expected to lose mass as Cu dissolves; it does not reduce the mass plated.
A more concentrated solution would not reduce the copper plated by a given charge.

items.q: Doubling which quantity, with everything else unchanged, halves the mass of metal plated?
options: The current through the cell
The time the current runs
The molar mass of the metal plated
The number of electrons needed by each metal ion

why.correct: mass = (I t / F) × (1 / electrons per ion) × molar mass. Only the electrons per ion is in the denominator.
options: Doubling the current doubles the charge, which doubles the mass plated.
Doubling the time doubles the charge, which doubles the mass plated.
Same moles, but each mole weighs twice as much: the mass doubles.
Right: twice the electrons per atom means half the moles of metal for the same charge.

items.q: In the plating of copper from Cu²⁺, which sequence of conversions takes you from current and time to mass?
options: I × t → coulombs → × F → mol e⁻ → × 2 → mol Cu → × 63.55 → g Cu
I × t → coulombs → ÷ F → mol e⁻ → ÷ 2 → mol Cu → × 63.55 → g Cu
I ÷ t → coulombs → ÷ F → mol e⁻ → ÷ 2 → mol Cu → × 63.55 → g Cu
I × t → coulombs → ÷ F → mol Cu → × 63.55 → g Cu

why.correct: q = It; mol e⁻ = q/F; mol Cu = mol e⁻ ÷ 2; mass = mol × molar mass.
options: Multiplying by F and by 2 inverts two steps: coulombs ÷ F give mol e⁻, and mol e⁻ ÷ 2 give mol Cu.
Right: charge, then moles of electrons, then moles of metal through the half-reaction, then mass.
Charge is current × time, not current ÷ time.
This skips the 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cu step, which doubles the answer.
